canonical_statement: The study tests whether a single language model can improve by jointly learning to generate adaptive executable training environments and solve them through self-play.
SPADE uses one shared language model in two prompted roles: an Environment Designer that writes executable environments and a Reasoning Agent that acts in them.
Each generated environment is a Python program implementing a Gym-style reset()/step() interface with state transitions and a reward function.
For each environment, the Environment Designer also emits a privileged hint that the Reasoning Agent receives only in the hinted evaluation arm.
The Environment Designer reward uses hint-based regret, defined as the Reasoning Agent's mean return with the privileged hint minus its mean return without the hint over fresh rollouts.
High hint-based regret is interpreted as a learnable-frontier environment, low regret with high return as mastery, and low regret with low hinted return as an intractable environment.
The hint-generation prompt requests the key strategy and expected answer format but forbids revealing the exact answer.
Both the Environment Designer and Reasoning Agent update the shared policy with GRPO using role-specific rewards.
In corpus-grounded games runs, every environment-generation round conditions on freshly sampled material from a 15,000-document corpus consisting of 10,000 mathematics and 5,000 science documents.
The environment memory stores prior environments annotated with regret scores and skill tags so the designer can reuse high-regret seeds and avoid examples that were too easy or too hard.
At each regeneration, the prior active environment set is replaced; the environment memory uses oldest-first eviction at a 200-record cap, and generation retries up to five times per environment.
Every generated environment must pass a programmatic smoke test that instantiates the class, calls reset(), and steps probe actions, rejecting candidates that fail to parse or crash.
Tool-use environments add a deterministic reset gate for success criteria and an LLM feasibility screen that rejects unreachable, pre-satisfied, or underivable success conditions.

The games curriculum uses 24 environments per rollout, with eight environments for each of three active skills drawn round-robin from six cognitive-skill categories, and regenerates every four rollouts.

Tool-use environments contain simulated OpenAI-format tools, mutable backend state, and three to five sequential natural-language instructions, with reward granted only when every instruction is completed.
The main experiments train Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 for 400 rollouts of 24 environments each.
The games evaluation holds out all benchmarks from training and measures AIME 2025, AIME 2026, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench-v6, and four hard Reasoning-Gym categories.
Two fixed-environment baselines are retrained from the same base model for 400 iterations: GRPO on the official RLVE environment set and GRPO on a static GPT-5.5-generated environment set.

Published AgentScaler, Agent-World, AWM, and EnvScaler tool-use scores are contextual reference rows rather than matched controls because their authors used different base models, training data, budgets, benchmark variants, or evaluation harnesses.
The canonical games configuration uses a constant learning rate of 1e-6, Adam with beta values 0.9 and 0.98 and weight decay 0.1, group size 16, and a maximum of 25 turns per episode.
On the eight-benchmark games suite, Qwen3-4B improved from a base mean of 38.9 to 44.1 after SPADE training, a reported gain of 5.2 points.

canonical_statement: Removing environment memory reduced the selected eight-benchmark games mean from 58.3 for full SPADE to 53.2.
Removing corpus grounding reduced the selected eight-benchmark games mean from 58.3 for full SPADE to 53.5.
Freezing Environment Designer training while also removing memory produced an eight-benchmark mean of 40.5, which was 9.7 points below the untrained base mean of 50.2.
A fixed GPT-5.5 Environment Designer with corpus grounding and memory reached an eight-benchmark mean of 53.0, compared with 58.3 for full SPADE.
The EMA learning-potential Environment Designer reward reached an eight-benchmark mean of 55.9, compared with 58.3 for hint-based-regret SPADE.
A two-skill curriculum reached an eight-benchmark mean of 53.7, compared with 58.3 for the six-skill curriculum.

canonical_statement: All 3,310 generated environments in the canonical 30B games run had distinct program hashes; the analysis also reported 2,388 distinct initial states and 1,513 distinct seed documents.

Qualitative rollout analysis reports a shift from long front-loaded derivations and repeated format failures early in training toward shorter evidence-gathering interactions and later derivation after sufficient evidence.

The Environment Designer cannot generate environments more complex than its base model and context budget can express, so reachable environment complexity is bounded by model scale and generation budget.
SPADE uses a fixed human-authored GRPO optimizer for both roles and does not learn or modify its own learning rule.

Hint-based regret is theoretically motivated but is not proven to produce an optimal curriculum, and the reported evaluation uses fixed benchmarks rather than an open-ended measure of reasoning growth.

The published tool-use comparison rows from other environment-synthesis systems are not controlled head-to-head comparisons because benchmark versions, user simulators, base models, training data, budgets, and harnesses differ.
Per-environment scalar rewards are not retained in the public run log, so the extended analysis measures learnability at the training-step level rather than per generated environment.
The environment-quality LLM rubric measures absolute difficulty and coherence rather than fit to the current Reasoning Agent.

In generated tool-use environments, validation checks do not always bind every qualifier in an instruction to the success criterion, so some criteria can miss details such as which account should pay an invoice.
The authors report releasing training and evaluation code, configuration files for every reported run, evaluation output JSON files, and scripts used to produce every figure.
The acknowledgments report support from academic-industry gift programs, research grants, philanthropic funders, corporate sponsors, and DARPA/AFRL contract FA8650-23-C-7316.

The authors conclude that making environment design a learnable self-play role can maintain gains after fixed environment pools saturate and can improve both held-out reasoning/code benchmarks and multi-step tool-use benchmarks.
